consensus_summary: Dogs predominantly symbolize uncleanness, contempt, moral impurity and exclusion from the holy/covenant community, commonly applied (contextually) to Gentiles/outsiders, false teachers, apostates, the wicked and hostile enemies.
book_summary: Dogs symbolize the Gentile power: an unclean beast outside the covenant table, fed on crumbs until brought in; the dogs that compassed and pierced at the cross; and those outside at the end.
consensus_core_identification: unclean outsiders/excluded persons or groups (Gentiles, wicked, false teachers, apostates, enemies)
book_core_identification: the Gentile power (unclean beast outside the covenant)
boundary_disagreement: Book fixes the primary referent as Gentile power across a salvation-historical arc (crumbs, cross, final outside), whereas consensus treats the image more flexibly for multiple unclean/hostile groups by context and does not privilege a single political or ethnic power.
material_contradiction: None; Gentile-as-dog is already a recognized common application inside the consensus range.
rationale: Consensus core is the negative valence of uncleanness and covenant-exclusion with several overlapping applications (Gentiles prominent among them). The book preserves that general category and the key texts but materially narrows the central identification to “the Gentile power” alone and organizes the cases around that single referent. This is boundary refinement (narrowing/subset), not replacement of the core or novelty, since the Gentile reading is already listed as common; broader cases such as false teachers remain outside the book’s primary claim.
strongest_objection: Fixed identification as Gentile power leaves unaccounted the equally prominent NT uses for false teachers (Phil 3:2) and apostates (2 Pet 2:22), which the consensus treats as parallel applications of the same negative symbol.
